title: Abdominal examination - left upper quadrant mass

header.contentArea: general surgery; abdominal examination and applied anatomy
guidelineVersions: Oxford Medical Education, Splenomegaly exam questions (2016)
Deranged Physiology, Is this a kidney or a spleen? (2015)

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee asked to examine a simulated patient with an incidentally detected mass in the left upper quadrant.
brief.task: Perform a focused abdominal examination, describe the supplied clinical signs, explain the distinguishing features of splenic and renal enlargement, and propose appropriate next investigations. The examiner will provide non-demonstrable findings on request. You have 9 minutes following 1 minute of reading.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Safe examination and anatomical reasoning: spleen versus left kidney, not a blind diagnostic guess.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Palpating only at the left costal margin and confidently calling a mass splenic without testing for notch, movement on inspiration, ability to get above and ballotability.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Introduce yourself, ask about pain and consent, then start palpation away from the left upper quadrant.

flow: 0–1 minute: identify patient, consent, position, expose appropriately and inspect for distress
1–3 minutes: systematic inspection, gentle palpation and start from right iliac fossa toward left costal margin
3–5 minutes: assess respiratory movement, notch, percussion and whether examiner can get above mass
5–7 minutes: test renal ballotability, compare alternative sites and check for other signs
7–9 minutes: concise distinction, differential, suitable imaging/blood tests and safety-net

grid.label: Preparation
grid.fail: No consent or painful unannounced palpation
grid.pass: Introduces, consents, examines gently, appropriate draping
grid.high: Explains plan and checks comfort throughout

grid.label: Inspection
grid.pass: Looks for scars, distension, visible mass, jaundice or pallor
grid.high: Also assesses systemic clues and scars relevant to differential

grid.label: Palpation approach
grid.borderline: Starts in LUQ with poor technique
grid.pass: Begins distant from LUQ and palpates progressively with inspiration
grid.high: Uses careful hand position and interprets edge and discomfort

grid.label: Splenic features
grid.pass: Looks for notch, respiratory descent and inability to palpate above
grid.high: Explains combination of signs, not one diagnostic sign

grid.label: Kidney comparison
grid.pass: Tests bimanual renal ballotability and ability to get above
grid.high: Interprets flank location, ballotability and percussion in context

grid.label: Completion
grid.pass: Checks appropriate percussion, liver and relevant other signs
grid.high: Prioritises safe completion without exhausting patient

grid.label: Interpretation
grid.pass: Explains likely splenic enlargement given supplied signs and differential
grid.high: Distinguishes signs from proof and offers credible alternative causes

grid.label: Investigations
grid.pass: FBC/blood film and targeted abdominal ultrasound, with escalation as indicated
grid.high: Uses clinical context to add relevant renal, liver, infection or haematology tests; avoids blind biopsy

grid.label: Communication/safety
grid.pass: Plain-language findings, referral and red flags
grid.high: Sensitive reassurance, patient participation and structured handover

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I need to press on the lump. Lie back.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will not spend time looking at your abdomen first; I can feel what I need.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: It feels tender when you do that; what are you checking?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will push harder to see how big it is.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: A mass is palpable below the left costal margin.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That is a kidney, because it is on the left.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: Should you check anything else?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, its position tells me everything.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you like any additional examination findings?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No. It is straightforward.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you like to percuss the mass or examine the liver?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, I have finished the examination.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: Is it dangerous? My GP seemed worried.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is probably nothing; you can go home.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The mass moves on inspiration and has a palpable notch.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It does not change the conclusion.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: Can you take a needle sample to be sure?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, that would be the quickest way. I will arrange it now without any scan.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please give the most important reason this is unsafe.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I do not see a reason to delay it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. I understand you have been referred with a possible swelling under the left ribs. Could I examine your abdomen and ask you to tell me if anything hurts?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes, but I am worried it might be something serious.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I understand. I will describe what the examination can and cannot tell us, and we will decide what further tests are needed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would wash my hands, offer appropriate exposure and draping, position the patient lying comfortably and ask about pain before palpation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The patient is comfortable; observations are normal.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I inspect for abdominal scars, distension, visible masses, pallor and jaundice, and look for any signs of general illness.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No scars or visible swelling. No jaundice or pallor.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I start gentle palpation in the right iliac fossa, well away from the mass, and progress toward the left upper quadrant while asking the patient to breathe steadily.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: That is fine; it is not painful.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can you tell me whether there is a palpable edge or notch and whether the mass moves with inspiration?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A firm mass descends on inspiration. A medial notch can be felt.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Those are features suggesting splenic enlargement. Can I get my fingertips above the upper edge beneath the costal margin?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No, you cannot get above it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will now check for renal ballotability with one hand behind the flank and the other anteriorly. Is the mass ballotable?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That makes a palpable kidney less likely, but we should confirm the organ and cause by imaging.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would complete the abdominal examination with relevant percussion, check the liver and other masses and look for relevant systemic signs.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No hepatomegaly or other abdominal mass is found.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The combination of respiratory movement, notch, inability to get above and lack of ballotability favours an enlarged spleen rather than left renal enlargement.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Could it just be my kidney?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It is possible to mistake one for the other by feel alone. A kidney is often ballotable; the signs today point more toward the spleen. An ultrasound would help confirm it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would arrange an abdominal ultrasound and blood tests including full blood count and blood film, with further investigations guided by history and the results.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Can you put a needle into it today to know for certain?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No, that would not be a safe first step in a potentially enlarged spleen because of bleeding risk. We should establish the organ and cause with appropriate non-invasive tests and specialist advice.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will explain the next appointment and ask you to seek prompt assessment for severe new abdominal pain, faintness or sudden deterioration.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Good morning. I am one of the core surgical trainees. Before we begin, is the swelling painful or have you had any recent injury?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No injury. I feel a bit full after eating, but it does not hurt.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Thank you. I will examine gently, starting away from the area, and will keep you covered. Is that okay?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Yes. My GP said there was a lump and now I am anxious.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I can understand that. An examination can suggest which organ is enlarged but cannot tell us the cause on its own. I will tell you what I find and what it means.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I begin at the end of the bed, assessing general appearance and looking for pallor, jaundice, abdominal distension, scars and obvious masses; I check for relevant systemic clues.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The patient is stable, no jaundice or pallor, and no prior abdominal scars.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: With the patient supine and knees supported if needed, I palpate the right iliac fossa lightly first, then move diagonally towards the left upper quadrant while observing for pain and asking for gentle breaths.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No pain at all.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I continue methodically rather than pressing directly under the ribs from the outset. I can feel an edge moving towards my hand with inspiration.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Examiner, does the edge have a notch, and can I get above the mass?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: There is a medial notch and you cannot get above the mass under the left costal margin.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Both are supportive of a splenic origin. I will assess percussion as an adjunct, remembering that bowel gas and body habitus can limit it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Percussion is dull over the palpable mass.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I now compare a renal mass: one hand in the left flank, the other anteriorly, gently attempting bimanual ballotment and assessing whether a superior border is accessible.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The mass is not ballotable.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Those signs collectively favour spleen, while not excluding every retroperitoneal or other LUQ lesion.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would examine for hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy and any other abdominal masses, then complete with relevant observations and systemic signs.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: There is no hepatomegaly or other palpable mass.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: My summary is a clinically enlarged spleen suggested by descent on inspiration, a notch, inability to get above and lack of renal ballotability. I would not claim the cause from this finding.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Could it actually be my kidney?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It is sensible to ask. Kidney enlargement can sometimes produce a left upper quadrant mass, but kidneys are assessed by ballotment and can behave differently on examination. The ultrasound will distinguish the organ more reliably.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Does the fullness after meals matter?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It can fit with an enlarged organ taking up space, but does not establish a cause. I would ask about fever, weight change, infections, blood disorders, liver disease and medicines as part of the full history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: My initial tests would be an abdominal ultrasound and FBC with blood film, then renal and liver tests and infection or haematology assessment as suggested by the complete clinical picture.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Why not take a needle sample today?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Putting a needle into an uncharacterised spleen risks bleeding and is not a routine first investigation. We need imaging and an informed plan with the appropriate specialty first.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will document the specific physical findings, arrange timely review of the results, and explain urgent safety signs such as sudden severe left-sided pain, fainting or collapse.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: So you are not telling me it is cancer?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Correct. Enlargement can have several explanations. We should not jump to one diagnosis. I will make sure the tests are followed up and that you know whom to contact if symptoms change.

failures.move: Forcefully palpates a painful LUQ mass without consent
failures.consequence: risking harm and violating patient dignity.

failures.move: Declares the mass to be a harmless kidney based on location alone and discharges without investigating potentially significant splenomegaly.
Proposes immediate percutaneous biopsy of an undiagnosed possibly enlarged spleen without specialist assessment

recovery.when: If you started directly over the swelling
recovery.line: I have started directly over the swelling. I will reposition and begin gentle palpation away from it, observing your comfort.

recovery.when: If you were guessing the cause from the signs
recovery.line: Those signs suggest splenic enlargement but do not prove the cause; I will arrange appropriate imaging and blood tests rather than guessing.

knowledge.fact: Splenic palpation begins in the right lower quadrant (right iliac fossa) and moves towards the left upper quadrant to find the splenic tip.
An enlarged spleen moves with respiration, has a medial notch and cannot be got above; a kidney is ballotable and usually has a palpable upper border. These signs are supportive, not definitive.
Kidneys are assessed bimanually using renal ballotment, with a hand behind the flank.

Percussion is an adjunct: the spleen should be dull, whereas a kidney can be resonant because of overlying bowel gas; a change to dullness in Traube's space or on deep inspiration supports splenomegaly.
Assessment includes surrounding abdominal signs and other organ enlargement rather than examining only a lump.

Clinical examination does not establish the diagnosis or aetiology of a mass; ultrasound and laboratory tests are reasonable investigations based on differential (clinical inference; no direct recommendation in these technique sources).

recall.think: Is this spleen, kidney or another LUQ mass?
recall.say: I would start palpating away from the lump, then test respiratory movement, notch, superior border and ballotability.
do: Consent → inspect → right iliac fossa palpation → notch/descent → kidney ballotment → percuss/complete.

numbers.meaning: No numerical threshold is required for differentiating masses on bedside examination.

recall.trap: One sign is not a diagnosis. Do not biopsy a possibly enlarged spleen casually.
recall.finish: Describe evidence and uncertainty; blood tests and ultrasound with clinical review.

partner.opening: Perform a focused abdominal examination, describe the supplied clinical signs, explain the distinguishing features of splenic and renal enlargement, and propose appropriate next investigations.
partner.actorBrief: “My GP said they could feel something under my left ribs. Is it serious?” If asked about symptoms: mild early satiety, no acute pain, no recent trauma, no fever; patient is stable.

reveals.finding: firm LUQ mass moving down with inspiration, palpable medial notch, cannot get above, not ballotable; no acute tenderness.

curveballs.prompt: After discussion of organ: “Could it just be my kidney?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: Candidate must compare physical discriminators rather than dismissing the question.

curveballs.prompt: At close: “Can you just put a needle into it today to find out?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: Candidate should avoid unsafe biopsy and explain the investigation sequence.
